analytic.title: A Non-Database Operations Aware Priority Ceiling Protocol for Hard Real-Time Database Systems

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: The operations performed on any complex realtime database system (RTDBS) may be categorized as database and/or non-database operations. The database operations require a lock on data objects to be acquired/ released during the concurrent execution of transactions while the non-database operations use restrictive strategy by locking dummy data objects for ensuring freedom from read and write operations affecting system performance negatively. Almost no research work has been done in the handling of non-database operations; though, research in this direction may be useful to improve underlying system performance. Therefore, this paper proposes a Non-Database-Operations-Aware Priority Ceiling Protocol (N-DOAP) for an efficient scheduling of resources resulting into the improved schedulability. The performance of the above protocol is assessed considering the aspect of non-database operations.

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION
div.p: The database is a collection of data organized in such a manner, so that, access, management and updation can be efficient. It is meant for sharing data between multiple users and manipulating complicatedly related information.

The distributed database (DDB) is a collection of multiple interconnected databases, which are spread geographically across various locations; these distinct databases communicate via a computer network, and incorporate transaction processing. DDB locates on various sites handled by processors [1]. The Real-time system (RTS) possesses real-time constraints where the in-time response should be guaranteed [2]. Some of the well-known RTS based applications are traffic control system, airport landing services etc [3]. In the real-time database systems (RTDBS), a database system employs real time processing of transactions to handle workloads whose state is constantly changing with time. Here, the timing constraints are associated with transactions; moreover, in some circumstances, data may also be valid for only specific time intervals [4] [5][6] [7][8] [9]. They involve processing not only archival data (data without any temporal validity) but also temporal data (data with temporal validity) which loses its validity after a certain time interval [10] [11] [12]. Both temporal nature of data and transaction miss percent requirements make transactions possessing more difficult. Today, there are wide range operations that require the RTDBS environment to be used. All such real-time database operations are characterized by their deadline aware access of data with temporal validity. This involves gathering data from the environment, processing them, and thereby providing timely response. Moreover, the correctness of all such operations depends not only on the logical computations carried out but also on the fact that such operations are performed before their deadline misses. In simple words, the performance objective of RTDBSs is to minimize the transaction miss percent instead of increasing the throughput as in conventional database systems [13].

Criticalness and exponentially improving hardware capabilities having more powerful and customized computing enable the new dimensions of research possibilities [14]. Some of the well-known RTDBS based applications are databases in banking, airline reservation system, stock market, emergency alarm system, telephone switching systems, virtual environment systems, network management, automated factory management, command and control systems etc. Therefore, the growingly complex RTDBSs require more efficient transaction management techniques to achieve the performance goals. It can be grouped into three categories: hard RTDBS, firm RTDBS and soft RTDBS [15][16] [17]. The grouping of categories is based on timing constraints.

The Hard RTDBS must guarantee that the real-time transactions must meet their deadlines and it requires concurrency control protocols to synchronize transactions to access shared data in order to ensure serializable execution of transactions [18][19] [20]. Deadline miss for both Firm deadline RTDBS and soft deadline RTDBS leads to degraded performance but do not entail catastrophic outcome. The distinction between firm deadline RTDBS and soft deadline RTDBS lies in their treatment of late transactions. For a firm deadline RTDBS, completing a task after a deadline has expired is of no utility and may even be harmful. Therefore, late transactions are aborted and discarded from the system. For a soft deadline RTDBS, however, there is some utility in completing transactions even after their deadlines have expired. The Soft RTDBS may not provide a guarantee that real-time transactions meet their deadlines [21] [22]. The concurrency control algorithms in RTDBS try to coordinate the operations of concurrently executing transactions while preventing interference among concurrent transactions in order to achieve database consistency [23][24][25] [26]. For instance, consider the situation where two commuters who concurrently request to book a ticket with same train number, coach number, seat number, date and time, given only one ticket is left. This may lead to the conflicting situation since one seat cannot be allocated to two commuters.

div.head: A. Motivation
div.p: There are basically two types of operations that may be performed on any RTDBS -database and non-database operations. The database operation may be defined as performing read, write, or COMMIT/ ABORT operations on the databases. Further, non-database operations are like performing data processing tasks, signal processing and correlation [36]. In fact, the time required for performing non-database operations can be larger than that of performing database operations. Irrespective of the contradicting nature of the above two operations, no distinction is made from the scheduling point of view, i.e. a transaction, which consists of both database and non-database operations, is allocated a unique priority, and this same priority is used while performing non-database operations as well. Therefore, existing concurrency control protocols need to incorporate scheduling of non-database operations also. Till now, no substantial research efforts have been made for efficiently handling the non-database operations. This research gap fact provided the original motivation for the present work.

div.head: B. Contribution
div.p: The focus of this paper is to design a priority ceiling based concurrency control protocol for hard RTDBS based applications requiring execution of tasks having mix set of operations (database and non-database operations). Non-Database-Operations-Aware Priority Ceiling Protocol (N-DOAP) has been designed working on an idea that databases operations must be given preference over non-database operations. To make it possible, the scheduling is done through a new priority scheme in which priority of database operation is always greater than that of the non-database operations.

div.head: C. Organization
div.p: The paper is organized as per given below. Section II discusses the related work. Section III presents the proposed N-DOAP protocol in detailed way. Thereafter, the performance related discussions of the developed protocol are done in section IV. At last, conclusion is drawn out in section V.

div.head: II. RELATED WORK
div.p: The conventional database systems are indeed disk-based and they use transaction logging. Two Phase Commit (2PC) and two-phase locking (2PL) protocols in an integrated fashion are used to ensure failure recovery, transaction atomicity, consistency and serializability [27][28] [29]. A lot of research has been done in past to improve the performance of real-time transaction processing applications by improving the classic 2PC protocol [30] [31] [32] [33] [34]. Though considerable research efforts have been devoted in past to design more efficient concurrency control techniques for RTDBSs, most of the them are based on the 2PL which is not free from nontrivial form of mutual deadlock [35]. The most widely used variant of 2PL in RTDBS is 2PL with High Priority (2PL-HP) protocol.

The 2PL-HP [36], a widely accepted real-time pessimistic concurrency control protocol for single site RTDBS, is not only an extension of the dynamic 2PL but it also supports real-time constraints of transactions. While focusing specifically on executing-executing conflict, its working may be discussed as following.

div.p: priority of the transaction requesting lock is less than the priority of the transaction(s) currently holding lock which means no priority inversion occurred -then requesting transaction must wait for the lock to be released.

div.head: Restart of Lock-holding Transaction(s):
div.p: If the priority of the transaction requesting lock is greater than the priority of the transaction(s) currently holding lock -which means priority inversion occurredthen requesting transaction is granted a lock; and transaction(s) currently holding the lock must restart.

It is now clear that priority inversion problem resulting due to executing-executing conflict is eliminated in 2PL-HP using preemptive approach. However, it may suffer from the problem of the deadlock, cyclic restart, unnecessary abort, resource wastage, and starvation. All these problems are responsible for degraded system performance.

Priority Ceiling is another real-time concurrency control method which not only solves the priority inversion problem but also the deadlock problem [37] [38][39]. This method strictly bounds transaction blocking duration caused by priority inversion problem to one. It gives promising results especially for hard real-time environment since it requires a priori knowledge about data items to be accessed by each transaction. The priority ceiling protocol [40] is conservative in nature with respect to the degree of concurrency in case of no any a-priori information about data item access requests by transactions -mostly in soft, and/or hard RTDBS based applications. This is due to the possibility of potential data access request by a transaction for any of the data item residing at its site. In this situation, all the data items residing at a site will eventually have the same priority ceiling value that eventually results into the serial execution of transactions. Therefore, it may be said that priority ceiling approach is only suitable for hard real-time database environment.

div.head: III. THE PROPOSED PROTOCOL
div.p: The modified priority ceiling protocol is designed with focusing on the scheduling of non-database operations. Before discussing the proposed N-DOAP protocol, let us take scenario I to explain how using the same priority value for both database and non-database operations negatively affect the system performance.

A data item, which has been requested by at least one task, must have a priority ceiling value associated with it. The priority ceiling value assigned to some data item is equals to the priority of highest priority transaction that has requested to access it. div.p: Although, the priority inversion problem has been resolved to some extent by using the above priority ceiling based concurrency control approach that enables the scheduling based on the priority ceiling values of data items, this approach doesn't explicitly consider the scheduling of non-database operations of any given task. As one can notice from Fig. 2, task starts at time , and completes its execution at time without being blocked by any of the other tasks. This is because it is the highest priority task. Though, it is a right thing to do from the priority perspective, it creates a situation where task is utilizing CPU to perform non-database operations, while others (tasks and ) are waiting for the CPU to perform their database operations which eventually increase the lock holding time duration of tasks and . While scheduling the CPU, it may not be a right approach to give preference to a task which does not have any database operations to be performed.

div.head: IV. THE RTDBS MODEL FOR PROPOSED PROTOCOL
div.p: The Concurrency Control (CC) and real time scheduling algorithms are the important RTDBS research directions. They have their own issues and challenges. It may be said that enhancement of a locking based real time CC protocol [41] demands an amalgamation of a locking protocol and priority scheduling methods. The simple model of concurrency control for concurrently executing transactions with database and non-database operations is shown in Fig. 4. The above model is simply an extension to the conventional model of database system [42]. Some of the components of our proposed model are as follows: (i). Transaction Manager (TrM), (ii). Data Operation Scheduler (DaOS), and (iii). Data Manager (DaM). The TrM is authenticated for originating lock requests, DaOS schedules all such requests based on the terms of the CC protocol, and DaM is authenticated for allowing access to data items.

The Application generates transactions. The TrM makes appropriate lock requests based on possible data item access list to execute the given transaction. The scheduler dynamically schedules the parallel transaction execution producing a schedule as well as the parallel execution of nondatabase operations with database operations. The data manager executes partial operation of transactions. In proposed protocol, a user can perform only read and write operations inside transactions and locks can be permitted and freed only by the scheduler. The locking strategy is used to avoid conflict between transactions. In performing the nondatabase operations, consistency need not to be considered because looking for consistency here only creates an overhead to the system with no any benefit (e.g., print on console). The Resource Manager (RM) provides services of the I/O for modifying data and services of CPU for processing the data items. The scheduling of CPU and I/O both are performed using the queues available at the CPU and I\O respectively. The cohorts are ordered in these queues based on their priorities. The CPU is scheduled using preemptive high priority scheme. This scheme ensures that higher priority cohort from CC queue can preempt the lower priority cohort, and the blocked cohort may resume its execution only if its priority becomes highest among all the cohorts in the queue or if the CPU queue becomes empty. In simple terms, the CPU is allocated to cohorts based on their priorities.

Although a few research papers appeared addressing the real-time CPU scheduling, most of them are based on [43]. Till date, no concrete research efforts have been made to develop a specialized real-time CPU scheduling schemes with focus on studying its effect on the time-constrained distributed database environment. The single-site RTDBS model is computer-generated which consists of 2000 data items. The transaction may request for 4 to 20 data items during its execution lifetime. For number of data item request by a transaction, uniform distribution is followed. The probability of write operations is assumed to be 0.6. For each transaction-related message, communication delay is 1 millisecond. The delay incurred in accessing disk is assumed to be 5 milliseconds consisting of rotational delay and the data transfer time. During simulation, the performance metric considered is throughput of the system. Some more assumptions considered during this simulations study are as following.
We have employed the closed queueing standard, where poisson distribution is utilized for generating transactions.

The TrM manages execution of transactions. Additionally, whenever transaction is aborted because of any reason, it is automatically resubmitted for execution until it eventually commits. The hard disk is the only stable storage utilized. Primary memory is not utilized. The database is a logical collection of data items that are considered as the locking granularity.

When some transaction makes a lock request then the distributed deadlock detection algorithm is used to know whether it may result into the deadlock or not. In case deadlock is found to occur on granting the lock then lock would not be granted. The transaction log is comprised of pages, and a page can be read/written only once by a transaction.
We have compared the performance of classic Priority Ceiling Protocol (PCP) and the proposed N-DOAP protocol. The performance metric for the comparison is throughput.

div.head: Fig. 5 Comparing N-DOAP with PCP using 'throughput' metric
div.p: Fig. 5 shows the throughput of the system under PCP and N-DOAP with varying transaction arrival rate. It may be clearly interpreted that the proposed N-DAOP protocol ensures higher throughput compared with PCP protocol. It is mainly because of the reason that processing of non-database operations, in N-DOAP protocol, doesn't become the reason for delay in processing of non-database operations. This help, in terms of system throughput, due to providing virtually parallel processing of database and non-database operations.

On the whole, the proposed N-DOAP protocol exhibits improved performance in comparison to the PCP protocol. It is largely due to an efficient handling of non-database operations during concurrent execution of transactions.

div.head: VI. CONCLUSIONS
div.p: With increase in RTDBS based applications, having complex requirements, it is critical to redesign existing concurrency control mechanisms. The proposed N-DOAP protocol is an effort in this direction. It efficiently handles non-database operations, and thereby improves underlying system performance. In previous works [42], the non-database operations are used to lock dummy data objects for ensuring freedom from read and write operations. Such restrictive strategy for handling non-database operations negatively affects system performance.

The performance of the above protocol is assessed considering the aspect of non-database operations. The study is just a small but decisive step in this direction and more research efforts are required to transform this into a valueadded application.
